name: Alkaline cooking of maize at San Bartolo
summary: Starch residues in sealed Maya household refuse pits at San Bartolo point to alkaline maize preparation and the disposal of its wastewater.
description: Researchers identified residues consistent with lime-treated maize in two pits at Grupo Zacatal, a Maya residential group at San Bartolo in Petén, Guatemala. They interpret the deposits as likely including wastewater discarded after preparing maize.

places.note: Grupo Zacatal residential group at San Bartolo, Petén. The map uses the registered country location.

date.label: Most likely c. 770–895 cal CE
date.basis: Santini et al. estimate the pits’ most likely use interval from charcoal dates and their stratigraphic relation to later sealing floors.

events.statement: Starch spherulites in sealed refuse deposits associated with Structures 192 and 195 B/C match residues produced by experimental lime treatment of maize. The excavators interpret the residues as likely discarded cooking liquid.
events.scope: Two bedrock pits in the residential group, each sealed by later construction.
events.population: Classic Maya residents of Grupo Zacatal
events.caveats: The dating is contextual and the charcoal ranges include intervals outside the authors’ preferred estimate. The deposits establish where the residues ended up. The precise cooking location, recipe and date of invention remain unresolved.

evidence.supports: The sealed household refuse contexts and the authors’ most likely interval of pit use, c. 770–895 cal CE.
Microscopic structure and a calcium-rich elemental signature support the identification. The authors infer that alkaline cooking liquid may have been discarded into the pits.
Lime-treated maize yielded distinctive spherulites under these experimental conditions. Non-alkaline controls did not. The archaeological study shares an author with the experiment.

earliest_record.rationale: The archaeological evidence establishes alkaline maize preparation in the local residential context during the likely pit-use interval.

caveats: How the San Bartolo community acquired or developed the practice remains unknown.

unresolved.note: A second team found similar residues at La Corona in vessel and grinding-stone samples. Securely dated earlier contexts and evidence tying preparation practices across communities would be needed to trace their relationship.

evidence.supports: The separate La Corona study places some practice evidence in the seventh and eighth centuries CE. Its sample-level chronology requires full-text review.

research.note: The event concerns a documented local case of maize preparation in a Maya residential group. The broader circumstances of invention or adoption remain unresolved.
